cards.title: Short Sentences, Short Words, Short Paragraphs
cards.summary: Use one idea per sentence, ~11 words on average, and mostly one-syllable words to keep readers moving through sales copy.
cards.use_when: Formatting the body copy of a product landing page, sales email or catalog ad where you need prospects to read every selling point.

cards.title: Personal Pronoun Density for Warm Copy
cards.summary: Load headlines and body copy with 'you' and 'I' to turn mass advertising into personal communication.
cards.use_when: Drafting headlines, product descriptions or email subject lines that currently sound distant and corporate.

cards.title: Feature-to-Benefit 'Big Deal' Translation
cards.summary: Convert every product spec into a WIIFM benefit by forcing each feature through the 'You benefit by…' test.
cards.use_when: Writing PDP bullets, bundle descriptions or ad copy from a spec sheet that currently lists only features.

cards.title: Biggest Benefit in the Headline
cards.summary: Put the single most important buyer benefit in the headline so 60% who only skim headlines still get the selling message.
cards.use_when: Writing or revising headlines for paid ads, emails, product pages or category banners.

cards.title: Short vs. Long Headline Trade-off
cards.summary: Shorter headlines are read more, but readability does not guarantee effectiveness — benefit outweighs brevity.
cards.use_when: Choosing between a compact and a long, information-heavy headline for an ad, email subject line or PDP hero.

cards.title: 22 Tested Headline Starters
cards.summary: Use a bank of proven opening words to set the tone of a headline while swapping in your specific product, offer and benefit.
cards.use_when: Stuck drafting headlines for a new product launch, promotion, category page or email campaign.

cards.title: 12 Openers That Bridge Headline to Body Copy
cards.summary: Pull the reader from the headline into the sales copy using one of 12 proven opening devices.
cards.use_when: The headline works but the body copy starts flat on a landing page, sales email or catalog ad.

cards.title: Break the Rectangle: Shape and Scroll-Stopping Design
cards.summary: Use shape difference — circular ads over the dominant square/rectangle — to stand out from competing placements.
cards.use_when: Placing display ads in a feed, marketplace or newsletter where your creative will sit cluttered among competitors.

cards.title: Never Reverse Long Body Type
cards.summary: White (or light) type on a dark background cuts legibility and slows reading — reserve it for short, large headlines.
cards.use_when: Reviewing a website, email or ad creative with dark backgrounds behind text.

cards.title: Extreme Specificity: Educate the Shopper With Detail
cards.summary: Describe your product's process, materials and numbers in exhaustive specifics so your listing feels more substantial than generic competitors.
cards.use_when: Writing a product page, brand story or category copy where competitors all use the same vague 'quality ingredients' language.

cards.title: Ogilvy Two-Thirds Layout and Caption Rule
cards.summary: Structure ads and hero sections with a dominant visual, headline below it, and copy beneath — plus a selling caption under every image.
cards.use_when: Designing a display ad, print insert or a PDP/landing-page hero where the image-to-copy balance needs a proven arrangement.

cards.title: Typeface Choice for Ease of Reading
cards.summary: Choose readable faces — serif for printed body text, initial caps for headlines — to prevent large chunks of readers abandoning copy.
cards.use_when: Specifying fonts for a catalog, print flyer, packaging, or the body text of a website or landing page.

cards.title: Deadlines and Scarcity to Beat Buyer Inertia
cards.summary: Add a hard or soft deadline to every offer so prospects act while the salesperson is still in front of them.
cards.use_when: Finalizing a promotion, launch, restock or cart-abandon email where the CTA currently has no reason to act now.

cards.title: Repeating 'You Learned' to Escalate Credibility
cards.summary: Use repeated paragraph leaders that echo the promise to speed reading, add tempo and imply volume of proof.
cards.use_when: Writing sales-page, webinar-recap or follow-up email copy where you need to consolidate the argument and drive the reader onward.

cards.title: Choose headline and body type size for on-screen readability
cards.summary: Pick initial-cap headlines, Arial/Verdana sizing, and dark-on-light color to maximize online reading speed for ads and landing pages.
cards.use_when: Formatting headlines, body copy or a landing-page hero for on-screen reading (PDP, ad, email) where legibility affects completion.

cards.title: Hire a real designer instead of self-designing sales materials
cards.summary: Use a vetted freelance designer or art-school student and always review samples before paying, because graphic software skills are not design skill.
cards.use_when: Producing product images, ad creative, packaging or sales collateral where amateur design risks a low-quality brand impression.

cards.title: Use questions to pull readers through copy
cards.summary: Open headlines, subheads and body copy with questions, especially 'Do you want...?' followed by a benefit, to keep prospects reading.
cards.use_when: Writing a product page, ad, email or sales letter where you need to hold attention from the headline into the body.

cards.title: Make sales letters personal, brochures detailed
cards.summary: Treat the sales letter as a one-on-one salesperson that meets prospects in their world, and the brochure as the sample-filled briefcase of complete details.
cards.use_when: Planning an email or sales letter versus a catalog/brochure, or deciding how personal versus detailed each piece of a campaign should be.

cards.title: Write teasers that survive the trash can
cards.summary: Design outer envelopes/carrier copy to look personal, not informational, so prospects open before trashing.
cards.use_when: Designing the subject line and sender presentation for a direct-mail or email campaign to a cold or loosely targeted list.

cards.title: Build a Granny-style response device
cards.summary: Convert order forms into warm, easy-to-complete 'Personal Trial Certificates' with guarantee, scarcity and a business reply envelope.
cards.use_when: Designing a cart, order form or checkout page to reduce friction and lift completion rate.

cards.title: Collect testimonials systematically with permission
cards.summary: Request testimonials with a specific questionnaire and a signed usage release, compensating with copies of the finished piece or a small payment.
cards.use_when: Sourcing social proof for a product page, ad or brochure and needing documented permission to use customer quotes.

cards.title: Use the Guillotine Principle to grab attention with a face
cards.summary: Place a close-up human face looking directly at the reader in ads and pages to gain attention, warmth and trust.
cards.use_when: Choosing the main image for an ad, PDP, packaging or landing-page hero where stopping power and warmth matter.

cards.title: Sharpen copy with powerful visual adjectives (PVAs)
cards.summary: Replace generic product descriptions with concrete, sensory adjectives that let prospects picture and mentally demo the product.
cards.use_when: Rewriting commodity product or service descriptions where your offer looks like competitors' and needs to stand out.

cards.title: Direct mental movies through the five senses (VAKOG)
cards.summary: Ramp up sensory detail across visual, auditory, kinesthetic, olfactory and gustatory channels so prospects mentally rehearse using the product before buying.
cards.use_when: Writing long-form sales copy, product pages or emails that must move a prospect from facts to purchase.

cards.title: Battle inertia by making buying easy and asking for action
cards.summary: Lower effort on every step and make an explicit call to action, since people are lazy and avoid involvement.
cards.use_when: Optimizing checkout, signup, quote request or any conversion flow where prospects stall or abandon.

cards.title: Differentiate with a unique selling proposition (USP)
cards.summary: Craft a real, truth-based gimmick or system that distinguishes your offer, since indistinguishable products give buyers no reason to prefer you.
cards.use_when: Positioning a product or store in a crowded category where your offer reads like generic sugar or salt.

cards.title: Positioning: turn a commodity into a category of one
cards.summary: Reframe your store from a generic product category into a distinctive, ownable identity so you stop blending in with competitors.
cards.use_when: You are writing your homepage headline, brand tagline, or About/positioning statement for a store that currently describes itself generically (e.g. 'quality home goods store').

cards.title: Make your ad hook 'specifically unique' instead of vague
cards.summary: Use concrete, specific, unexpected hooks instead of generic category claims to earn more readership and clicks.
cards.use_when: You are drafting ad creative or a product landing page headline in a crowded category where every competitor uses the same generic promise.

cards.title: Build an authority position and make content as the evidence
cards.summary: Become the recognized expert in your niche by publishing knowledge in many formats, which lowers buyer skepticism and builds trust before purchase.
cards.use_when: You want your store to be seen as the go-to expert in a niche, and you need to convert expertise into a concrete content and trust-building plan.

cards.title: Use a customer survey as a sales letter in disguise
cards.summary: Mail a short survey with an exclusive thank-you offer embedded to collect buyer insight and generate an easy incremental sale.
cards.use_when: You want to know what customers actually think and, at the same time, drive a repeat purchase or upgrade with minimal friction.

cards.title: Format a survey for maximum response
cards.summary: Use a double postcard or one-page letter with a postage-paid reply envelope and mostly multiple-choice questions to maximize survey returns.
cards.use_when: You are physically mailing survey cards or letters to your customers and need the highest possible reply rate to make the feedback useful.

cards.title: Use 'grabbers' to force attention on your direct mail or package inserts
cards.summary: Attach a small physical object to your mailer or insert to create curiosity and a sense of obligation to read your offer.
cards.use_when: You send physical mail to prospects or include marketing inserts in shipments and need something that makes your piece stand out in the stack.

cards.title: Long copy outsells short copy—if you keep it interesting
cards.summary: Well-written long copy beats short copy because it satisfies both detail-hungry buyers and quick deciders, online and offline.
cards.use_when: You are deciding how much copy a sales page, product page, or email should carry, especially in a high-consideration purchase.

cards.title: Make your ad look like editorial content to lift readership
cards.summary: Camouflage ads in the typeface, column width, and news voice of the publication so more readers stop and read.
cards.use_when: You place ads in newspapers, newsletters, or niche publications where ad blindness is high and you want higher readership.

cards.title: Wrap important offers in a coupon border to trigger savings associations
cards.summary: Surround an order form, bonus, or reply device with a broken coupon-style border to leverage conditioned 'savings' associations.
cards.use_when: You are designing order forms, bonus boxes, or reply coupons on a landing page, print ad, or email and want to increase response.

cards.title: Match images to product and use them to demonstrate
cards.summary: Show the product in use, with people and context, to lift readership and clicks over plain product or no-image ads.
cards.use_when: You are choosing hero images and creative for product pages, ads, or landing pages and want to maximize attention and relevance.

cards.title: Use visual density and large formats to lift ad readership
cards.summary: Ads with more visual elements and larger formats get seen and read more than sparse or standard-sized ads.
cards.use_when: You are planning ad layout, banner sizing, or the visual-to-text ratio of a paid placement and want to boost noted/read-most metrics.

cards.title: Test offers systematically, not just copy
cards.summary: If ads or pages underperform, revise the offer itself—framing, free extras, and segmentation—before abandoning the product.
cards.use_when: Your ad, product page, or email is underperforming and you have already tried headline changes but response is still weak.

cards.title: Ask the market before you build the promo
cards.summary: Survey your target market before spending on campaigns so you build around what they actually want, not what you assume.
cards.use_when: You are about to invest in a major promotion, new product launch, or seasonal campaign and want to de-risk it with research.

cards.title: Use editorial and survey assets again and again
cards.summary: Repetition and multi-format reuse of proven assets overcome the fact that any one insertion reaches only a fraction of your audience.
cards.use_when: You are planning media frequency or content repurposing and wonder whether to keep running a proven ad or asset.

cards.title: 7 online response boosters and their traps
cards.summary: Use email frequency, HTML vs. text, subject lines, ad format, animation, and specificity to lift online response—without confusing clicks for sales.
cards.use_when: You are designing an email campaign or banner ads and need concrete online response guidance rather than print-era assumptions.

cards.title: Position yourself before you position the product
cards.summary: Business positioning and offer positioning are two different jobs—do the business identity first, then customize each campaign's offer positioning.
cards.use_when: You are splitting time between building a brand identity and writing individual campaign or product offers and need to keep the two distinct.

cards.title: Specific Headlines Over Clever Headlines for Paid Ads
cards.summary: Write ad headlines that state the offer and audience plainly rather than chasing cleverness, because clicks for the wrong reason convert to sales far less often.
cards.use_when: Writing or reviewing headlines for paid social, search, or display ads and deciding between a clever hook and a specific offer-based headline.

cards.title: Run Multiple Ad Formations in One Placement for 1+1=3
cards.summary: Place more than one ad in the same issue or channel so repeated exposure compounds response, using proven right-page and spread formations.
cards.use_when: Planning ad frequency and placement for print inserts, catalog pages, or multi-ad buys where a single placement isn't generating traction.

cards.title: Offer Longer Guarantees to Increase Confidence and Reduce Returns
cards.summary: A strong, longer-than-competitor guarantee lowers pre-purchase stress, boosts conversion, and paradoxically lowers returns by removing the beat-the-clock mindset.
cards.use_when: Setting return, refund, or satisfaction policy on a product page, in ads, or in checkout, especially for high-ticket or unfamiliar products.

cards.title: Use Square-Root Rule to Decide Ad Size vs. Color
cards.summary: Attention grows roughly with the square root of ad area, so quadrupling size roughly doubles attention while color can be the cheaper attention lever.
cards.use_when: Budgeting between buying more ad space versus adding color or improving the ad's creative, for any paid placement where you can increase either size or color.

cards.title: Stop Worrying About Page Position, Except the Fantastic Four
cards.summary: Inside-page position (left/right, front/middle/back) barely affects ad effectiveness; only cover and specific high-attention slots justify premium placement.
cards.use_when: Negotiating premium placement rates for inserts, magazine ads, newsletters, or newsletters-like digital placements where you're deciding whether to pay extra for position.

cards.title: Choose Colors and Paper/Ink Combos by Measured Readership
cards.summary: Consumer color preference ranks blue, red, green, violet, orange, yellow; certain paper/ink and color pairings measurably improve or wreck readability.
cards.use_when: Specifying packaging colors, PDP/landing-page palette, ad backgrounds, and print insert paper/ink for maximum readership and shelf impact.

cards.title: Use Psychological Pricing: Fractional for Value, Round for Prestige
cards.summary: Odd/fractional price endings signal value while rounded whole numbers signal premium quality; the specific endings matter (99 > 95, 88 and 79 and 98 also signal value).
cards.use_when: Setting prices on product pages, bundles, cart upsells, and ad copy for mass-market versus premium tiers.

cards.title: White-Wrap Your Ad to Boost Attention Without More Copy
cards.summary: Buying more space and surrounding the original ad with white space increases attention more efficiently than filling the extra space with copy.
cards.use_when: Designing a PDP hero, landing-page module, or print ad where you can buy more space and are deciding between more content and more whitespace.

cards.title: Guarantee Credibility with Concrete Facts, Examples, and Specificity
cards.summary: Replace vague statistics with vivid examples and extreme specifics to build believability and make claims more persuasive.
cards.use_when: Writing PDP copy, testimonial sections, pitch decks for offer pages, and any proof blocks in ads or landing pages.

cards.title: Convert Feature Specs into Bottom-Line Benefits
cards.summary: Move past features into the single core benefit—the bottom-line outcome—and build copy around it in a logical Get-Attention → Interest → Desire → Proof → Action progression.
cards.use_when: Rewriting PDP descriptions, ad copy, and email body copy where the text is heavy with specs but light on why the customer should care.

cards.title: Wrap Copy With Short Sentences, Simple Words, and Serif/Sans Choice
cards.summary: Readability lifts response: short sentences, common words, thick paragraph breaks, personal pronouns, and matching typeface to medium (serif for print, sans-serif for web).
cards.use_when: Editing product descriptions, landing-page body copy, and email copy for readability and per-word impact.

cards.title: Build the Killer Ad Checklist Before Launch
cards.summary: Use the 46-point killer ad checklist as a pre-launch gate to ensure headline, body, layout, and proof elements are in place before spending on any ad.
cards.use_when: Reviewing any ad, PDP hero, or campaign creative just before publishing; a sanity gate to catch missing headline, proof, or CTA elements.

cards.title: Make Buying Ridiculously Easy, Every Step
cards.summary: Remove friction across the whole purchase path—channels, payment methods, guarantees, and installments—because ease is a measurable response lever.
cards.use_when: Auditing cart and checkout flow, payment options, contact methods, and order completion steps on an ecommerce store.

cards.title: Boost Coupon/Offer Returns With 11 Tactics
cards.summary: Eleven coupon-design tactics, from headline instruction to check-off boxes and arrows, to lift redemption of discounts and promos.
cards.use_when: Designing discount codes, promo banners, cart coupons, or insert coupons to maximize click and redemption.

cards.title: Use Fear, Identity, and Social Proof Ethically in Ad Copy
cards.summary: Multiple persuasion levers—fear, ego morphing, bandwagon, social proof, authority, commitment—can be layered into ads, each with a specific mechanism and risk.
cards.use_when: Choosing which persuasion angle to lead with in a paid ad campaign or landing page (e.g., fear-based for problem categories, identity-based for aspirational products).

cards.title: Match Message to Peripheral or Central Processing Audience
cards.summary: The Elaboration Likelihood Model says superficial thinkers respond to peripheral cues (visuals, authority, likability) while engaged buyers respond to central cues (evidence, arguments).
cards.use_when: Deciding whether an ad or PDP should lead with emotional/visual cues versus deep evidence, based on how motivated the target audience is.

cards.title: Test Offers, Headlines, and Message Sideness Before Scaling
cards.summary: Systematically test offers and ad components; frame messages with the right sidedness (one-sided vs. acknowledging counter-arguments) and use surveys before assuming you know the audience.
cards.use_when: Structuring A/B tests for PDPs, ad creatives, or offer variants before scaling spend; also for post-purchase surveys and review-based research.

cards.title: Run Deadline-Driven Urgency Without Cheating the Buyer
cards.summary: Deadlines, limited offers, and scarcity cues break inertia; use them honestly and match them to the buyer's stage.
cards.use_when: Designing cart-abandon, flash-sale, or limited-stock promo copy where urgency is the lever being applied.

cards.title: Use Testimonials, Photos, Captions, and Person-Looking Photos for Proof
cards.summary: Specific visual and proof conventions—real testimonials, action photos, captions, and a person's gaze—lift ad performance and reduce reader skepticism.
cards.use_when: Optimizing PDP images, testimonial sections, ad creative, and any place where visual proof supports conversion.

cards.title: Match Long Copy or Short Copy to the Buying Situation
cards.summary: Long copy works when the reader is engaged and the offer merits detail; short copy wins when the reader needs only a quick reason to act—test rather than assume.
cards.use_when: Choosing ad format or PDP body length for a specific category (e.g., impulse product vs. considered high-ticket purchase).

cards.title: Give Yourself a 'Cleverectomy' When Creative Argues With Performance
cards.summary: Reject creative for creative's sake; advertising is business communication whose purpose is to sell, and copy that impresses friends but not prospects wastes spend.
cards.use_when: Resolving disagreements between design/creative stakeholders and performance marketers over ad or PDP creative direction.

cards.title: Why Cold AI Hooks Fail (and the Copy-Paste Fallback Also Fails)
cards.summary: Generic LLM hook output is bland because the model isn't grounded in short-form social data, and cloning viral hooks across niches breaks on psychology, format and grammar.
cards.use_when: You are briefing AI (or a copywriter) to write paid-ad or organic video hooks for your store and wondering why output feels generic, or considering lifting a competitor's viral hook verbatim.

cards.title: The Four-Step Hook Machine Workflow
cards.summary: A four-step AI workflow — connect a data source, scrape top videos, sort winners from losers, extract psychological and grammatical rules — that yields a custom hook grading rubric and generator.
cards.use_when: You want a repeatable system for producing and grading short-form hooks for product ads or content, instead of writing each hook from scratch.

cards.title: Filter Brand Deals Out of Hook Analysis With a 2% Engagement Floor
cards.summary: Screen out any video below roughly 2% engagement before analyzing hooks, because paid spend inflates view counts and corrupts the winner data.
cards.use_when: You are assembling a set of top-performing competitor or own-brand videos to extract hook and creative principles from.

cards.title: Find the View Drop-Off Break Point to Separate Winners From Losers
cards.summary: Sort a channel's top 10 videos by views, locate the natural break point, and treat videos above it as the hook principles worth extracting.
cards.use_when: You need to decide which of your or a competitor's videos to study for ad hook and creative format patterns, and which are just baseline performers.

cards.title: Extract Hook Principles in Four Buckets (Psychology, Framing, Grammar, Non-Obvious)
cards.summary: Have the analysis classify winner-vs-loser differences into psychology, trigger words and framing, grammatical structure, and non-obvious takeaways — then turn them into rules.
cards.use_when: You are converting raw video performance data into concrete creative rules for writing product ad hooks or landing-page headlines.

cards.title: Don't Cross-Pollinate Creator Styles in One Analysis
cards.summary: Mashing multiple creators with different styles into a single analysis dilutes extracted hook principles toward an ineffective average.
cards.use_when: You are deciding whether to run one hook-extraction pass across several competitor accounts or separate passes per account.

cards.title: Build a Custom Hook Rubric From Data, Then Grade and Rewrite Draft Hooks
cards.summary: Combine a fixed set of universal storytelling principles with principles extracted from your data, then grade any new hook against that rubric and generate rewrites.
cards.use_when: You have drafted a hook for an ad or video and want a structured critique plus concrete alternative versions before spending on creative.

cards.title: Analyze Your Own Backlog First — Competitors Second
cards.summary: The strongest hook rubric comes from running the system on your own videos, then adding competitors one at a time rather than in a single mixed batch.
cards.use_when: You are setting up a long-term hook or ad-copy generation system for your store's content channels.

cards.title: Use Topic-Format Compatibility Screening Before Generating Hooks
cards.summary: Before generating hooks, filter winning formats by whether they fit the topic — forcing a stat/case-study template onto a conceptual topic reproduces the cross-pollination failure.
cards.use_when: You are generating ad hooks or video hooks for a specific product or concept and have a library of proven competitor formats available.

cards.title: Prefer Transcript-Based Analysis Over Lightweight Caption Scraping
cards.summary: Deep hook extraction depends on transcripts, visual layout and metrics — lightweight scraper connections only surface captions and rankings and miss the principles.
cards.use_when: You are choosing tooling to research creative for your store's ads and deciding how deep the analysis needs to go.

cards.title: Copywriting is sales in written form, not content or creative writing
cards.summary: Define copywriting for ecommerce as written sales persuasion distinct from SEO blogs, organic social and creative writing.
cards.use_when: Deciding how to brief or evaluate product page, ad and email copy on an ecommerce store.

cards.title: Treat the funnel as a mountain, not a slide
cards.summary: Map every micro-decision between ad impression and purchase because prospects can drop off at any single step.
cards.use_when: Diagramming the path from ad to PDP to cart for your store to find where prospects leak.

cards.title: Put the customer in the hero role, drop first-person pronouns
cards.summary: Rewrite copy to eliminate I/me/my/about-us framing so the reader stays the hero of their own story.
cards.use_when: Editing any store asset (PDP, ad, email, about section) that talks about the brand instead of the buyer.

cards.title: Use the email outline template to beat blank page syndrome
cards.summary: Pre-build a skeleton for each email with conversion goal, subject, preview text, story, content, CTA and PS before writing.
cards.use_when: Writing any launch, welcome or promotional email sequence for your store and staring at a blank page.

cards.title: Let drafts rest 24 hours and edit by reading out loud
cards.summary: Edit copy by sleeping on the draft, then reading aloud until you never stumble, looking for pronoun flip-flops, tangled syntax and repeated words.
cards.use_when: Editing store emails, ad copy or landing page drafts before they go live.

cards.title: Fix PPC messaging congruency between ad and destination
cards.summary: Match the promise, visuals and language of your ad to the exact page the click lands on so prospects are never surprised.
cards.use_when: Running paid social or search ads to a store page and seeing high bounce or low click-to-purchase.

cards.title: Write PPC and social ad creative for scrollers
cards.summary: Build ad copy for short attention: emojis, short lines, one-to-three-sentence paragraphs and reader-focused wording.
cards.use_when: Writing Facebook, Instagram or Google ad creative for a store and needing formats that stop the scroll.
